newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher on steady rate scenario.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher on steady rate scenario.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended higher on Wednesday as foreign and domestic investors purchased securities amid an outlook for steady interest rates.

"You had continued followthrough from Tuesday's action," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "The market is feeling comfortable with the notion that we'll be dealing with a 5-1/4 percent Federal funds rate until the next meeting."
Federal Reserve policymakers left rates unchanged at their September 24 gathering. Their next meeting is on November 13.

"Apparently people are feeling sort of bullet-proof right here because they feel the Fed ... is going to tolerate a little uptick in inflation and while that will cause problems in the long run, in the near-term, it's let the good times roll," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust.

"There may be some rethinking going on about the economic setting with people beginning to believe that the Fed might not tighten even in November," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
That view allowed rates to fall at the short end of the (maturity range) as well as the long end, said Moran.
Three- and six-month bill rates closed down four and eight basis points, respectively, to 4.93 percent and 5.07 percent.
Steve Ricchuito, chief financial economist at BZW Securities Inc. agreed the market advanced in response to the Fed's decision on Tuesday to hold interest rates steady.

"The talk going into FOMC time was that there was a lot of overseas money looking to get involved in the market even if the Fed tightened," Richhuito observed. That buying caught the Street short and people had to cover short positions, he said.

Traders said central bank buying and a large purchase of securities in the middle of the yield curve gave the market a leg up at mid-morning. They said the Fed purchased Treasuries for the accounts of other central banks.
A Fed spokesman said if the Fed were "doing any operations for a customer of ours, we would not comment." The Fed would neither confirm nor deny making purchases.

A well-bid Treasury auction of $18.25 billion in two-year notes also bolstered the market's positive sentiment, analysts said. The Treasury sold the notes at a high yield of 6.080 pct. The bid-cover ratio was a firm 2.64.
A dollar rally also enhanced the Treasury market's performance, analysts said.
"The dollar staged a nice rebound," said Flanagan. "It bounced right back overnight to close near its recent highs, especially against the yen," he said.
Dealers said the dollar rallied sharply against most currencies as investors poured funds into bond markets with relatively high interest rates in Italy and the United States.
On Thursday, the market will turn its attention to the first major piece of economic data it will get since Tuesday's Fed policy meeting -- the August durable goods orders report.
"The market looks good at the present time," said Flanagan. "But with each new economic statistic, we're going to go back and forth on whether the Fed will eventually move or not."
Year-bill rates fell three basis points to 5.37 percent.

Prices of two-year notes rose 3/32 to 100-2/32, yielding 6.09 percent. Five-year notes rose 8/32 at 100-7/32, yielding 6.45 percent and the 10-year note climbed 14/32 to 102-6/32 to yield 6.93 percent.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year Treasury bond advanced 23/32 to 97-24/32, yielding 6.93 percent at the close.
